Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Medal tally of India's athletes by birth state/UT

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

Uttar Pradesh and Delhi carry the same gloomy picture

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

How active are states/UTs with CWG medallists in promoting sport

Does it matter so much?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves.

Article Title: ‘Performance was not the reason’: Kaif questions Sarfaraz’s exile, backs him over Jurel for Sri Lanka Tests
Article Text:
Sarfaraz Khan (BCCI Photo)

Kaif picks Sarfaraz over Jurel for No. 6

Jurel's form opens the door

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former India cricketer Mohammad Kaif has welcomed Sarfaraz Khan 's return to India's Test squad and backed him to make the playing XI against Sri Lanka, arguing that his ability against spin could make him a better option than Dhruv Jurel in the conditions expected in Galle.Sarfaraz was added to India's squad as a replacement for injured Sai Sudharsan and joined the team in Sri Lanka on Monday. His return has also reignited the debate over his prolonged absence from the Test setup, having last played for India against New Zealand in November 2024.Kaif, while discussing Sarfaraz's comeback on his YouTube channel, questioned why the batter was left out after his initial run in the side. He stressed that poor performance was not the reason for Sarfaraz's exclusion."There was a reason he was not allowed to play. Performance was not the reason. There was no reason. That his runs were not getting made, that the bat was not working. He made runs against New Zealand. He came across the field. He was playing well. He was in form. When he scored against England, he had a good start," Kaif said.Kaif also praised the decision-makers for bringing Sarfaraz back, believing his skill against spin could prove valuable in Sri Lanka."Whatever happened in between, he was removed. But now, whoever said that he should come back, I feel that he is thinking for India. India is thinking for cricket. We have to win. We will need good players. We will need good players. We will need good players who play well," Kaif further said.He added: "So, first of all, whoever has named him on the table, I congratulate him a lot. And I hope that Sarfaraz Khan will go there and play well."The bigger question now is whether Sarfaraz can go straight into India's XI. Kaif believes he should, although he acknowledged that the team management could favour Jurel because of his existing involvement with the squad."If they follow the trend of backing the players who have already been playing for the team, then they might say, ‘Jurel has been with us already. He hasn’t scored consistently, but we will back him because he has already been part of the team.’ If that is the approach, then Sarfaraz will have to wait," Kaif said."But if you ask me what the best XI is, Sarfaraz’s name comes into my best XI because of his ability to play spin at No. 5 or No. 6. His record against spin is excellent," he added.Sarfaraz's range of strokes is another reason Kaif sees him as a strong option, particularly if the pitch becomes increasingly difficult to bat on as the Test progresses."He also has a wide range of shots. When you get to the fourth or fifth day, batting becomes more difficult, and that is where a player like Sarfaraz Khan can be very useful," he said. "He knows how to use sweeps and reverse sweeps effectively. He can hit over extra cover, he is good off the back foot and he attacks spin."Kaif also pointed to Jurel's recent form as another reason he would prefer Sarfaraz for the first Test."Look, I can understand that India have played well, but Jurel’s recent Test record and form haven’t been that great," Kaif said.The selection debate could become one of the key talking points ahead of the first Test, particularly with Sarfaraz now back in contention. India have a number of batting options, but Kaif's preference is clear: if the objective is to pick the XI best suited to the conditions, Sarfaraz should get the opportunity.Sarfaraz has played six Tests and scored 371 runs at an average of 37.10, including one century and three half-centuries. His standout innings came against New Zealand, when he scored 150.India will begin the two-Test series in Galle on August 15, before the second Test in Colombo from August 23. The No. 6 spot could be one of the most closely watched selection calls when the team walks out for the opening Test.
Article Summary: Sarfaraz was added to India's squad as a replacement for injured Sai Sudharsan and joined the team in Sri Lanka on Monday. His return reignited the debate over his prolonged absence from the Test setup, having last played for India against New Zealand in November 2024. Kaif questioned why the batter was left out after his initial run in the side. He stressed that poor performance was not the reason for Sarfaraz's exclusion.

Article Title: Doping blow: Deepanshu suspended, out of Asian Games
Article Text:
Image credit: Wrestling Federation of India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Indian wrestling has suffered a doping setback ahead of the Asian Games, with Greco-Roman wrestler Deepanshu provisionally suspended by the National AntiDoping Agency (NADA) after failing an out-of-competition dope test for the prohibited anabolic steroid stanozolol.Deepanshu, who competes in the 130kg category, had won the Asian Games selection trials in Lucknow and was part of the country’s squad for the continental showpiece. However, his positive test has resulted in his removal from the national camp and squad.Ronak Dahiya, who had lost to Deepanshu in the trials and was named as reserve, has now been drafted into the 130kg category.It has been learnt that Deepanshu’s sample was collected by dope control officers at the Lucknow camp. The sample was subsequently tested at the National Dope Testing Laboratory (NDTL), where it returned positive for stanozolol.The latest doping case is particularly serious as it is Deepanshu’s second offence. He had earlier served a threeyear ban for a doping violation involving the same prohibited substance.He returned to competition in 2025 and subsequently earned a place in the national camp. As a repeat offender, Deepanshu faces a potentially lengthy ban of up to eight years, which could put his career in jeopardy.His suspension has left Indian wrestling to deal with an embarrassing doping blow during a crucial phase of its preparations for the Games.Meanwhile, Ronak has begun training alongside the main Games squad and will travel to Uzbekistan along with other members of the Greco-Roman contingent for training-cum-exposure trip.The fresh doping setback comes on the heels of disciplinary action against Indian weightlifters selected for the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Three of the four lifters who tested positive for prohibited substances ahead of the Games have admitted their violations and accepted bans ranging from three to four years. Their suspensions have also extinguished their Asian Games hopes.
Article Summary: Greco-Roman wrestler Deepanshu has been provisionally suspended by the National AntiDoping Agency (NADA) He failed an out-of-competition dope test for the prohibited anabolic steroid stanozolol. As a repeat offender, he faces a potentially lengthy ban of up to eight years.

Article Title: BWF World Championships: Ayush Shetty up for Shi Yuqi challenge
Article Text:
Ayush Shetty

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Following his impressive runner-up finish at the Badminton Asia Championships (BAC) in April , Ayush Shetty has struggled to hit the same stride. A minor elbow injury in June did not help, and the Mangaluruborn shuttler has since suffered three first-round exits and two second-round defeats in the last three months.The road ahead is set to get even tougher. Ayush, ranked World No. 23, will face World No. 1 Shi Yuqi of China in the opening round of the World Championships. Last week, an intrigued Ayush followed the Worlds draw live. There was little reaction when he learnt that Shi would be his firstround opponent — perhaps understandable given the daunting challenge.The Chinese has beaten him in all three of their meetings and is among the favourites to defend his title. In their three encounters, Ayush has managed to take just one game off Shi, but the 21-year-old believes those defeats have also provided valuable lessons.“I will be more prepared and need to be tactically better this time,” said Ayush during a media interaction on Monday.“There’s no revenge kind of an emotion when I play (against Shi). But it’s a new tournament and a new match. It’ll be a tough battle, and you really have to work hard against him.”Playing in front of a home crowd brings its own pressures, but the lanky 6-foot-4-inch shuttler is embracing them.“There is pressure. But it’s more of excitement, you know, playing at home,” said the World No. 23 shuttler.
Article Summary: Ayush Shetty will face World No. 1 Shi Yuqi of China in the opening round of the World Championships. The Mangaluruborn shuttler has suffered three first-round exits and two second-round defeats in the last three months. The Chinese has beaten him in all three of their meetings.

Article Title: ‘Intensity is non-negotiable’: T Dilip reveals what still sets Virat Kohli apart in the field
Article Text:
Virat Kohli (Pic credit: BCCI)

‘The intensity is always contagious’

‘ Barbados 2024 ’ remains Dilip's most cherished memory

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former India fielding coach T Dilip has revealed what made Virat Kohli stand apart on the field, even at this stage of his career, describing the star batter's intensity as a quality that continues to push everyone around him to raise their standards.Reflecting on Kohli's influence during his five-year stint with the Indian team, Dilip said there was little difference between the former captain's approach during training and in matches — a trait that had a direct impact on his teammates."When it comes to Virat Kohli, intensity is non-negotiable. You have seen in power play how he is at your batsman at covers or short mid wicket with his reflexes, with his dives, with his stops. Even in the last series he was putting those dives and sharp at you all the time," Dilip said in a video shared by Star Sports.What impressed him most, however, was that Kohli's intensity was not limited to moments when the ball came his way."But what impressed me most is not the actions what he does when the ball is at him but also when the ball is not at him. You will see him running towards the non-striker and to take that throw and throwing back to the wicket keeper," Dilip explained.Dilip also highlighted Kohli's willingness to put himself in demanding fielding positions even late in an innings."Even at this juncture of his career, even today he goes to long on to long on in last overs and he is the first one to run out. And that's a fabulous thing to do as a team," he said.According to Dilip, Kohli's biggest contribution was the effect his approach had on the players around him."The intensity is always contagious when he is around. With Virat Kohli one thing you always see is there is not much difference between him in a practice session or a match. And that's very, very important because it's just not Virat Kohli who's fielding. There are five other players who are fielding with him who have stretched their limits when they are doing with Virat Kohli. That is the influence he has on the group actually. "Dilip, who signed off as India's fielding coach early in this month after a memorable five-year tenure, also picked India's 2024 T20 World Cup triumph in Barbados as his most cherished moment with the team."If I have to go back to my best moment, I think Barbados 2024. The silence for few seconds before it broke. I think in that silence I could sense the amount of hard work the boys have put in that four years. And I'll always keep that frame in my mind," he said.Dilip also took pride in how the fielding medal ceremony, introduced during the 2023 ODI World Cup, changed the team's attitude towards fielding. Rather than rewarding only spectacular catches, the ceremony recognised contributions across the field."What I thought was to recognize the impact overall as a fielder than just a spectacular catch. But what it brought in is then all the 11 players on the field that we may not be in the hot spot, but a little contribution would get me that award," Dilip said."Players started to notice small things they act on the field. They celebrated when their other teammates did. Because end of the day, fielding medal is a team award and players embraced it. Fans actually supported it. But I think overall, fielding did get the recognition what it deserved the most."Dilip's tenure coincided with one of India's most successful periods across formats, with the team winning the T20 World Cup in 2024 and 2026 and the Champions Trophy in 2025. He also witnessed India's Asia Cup triumphs in 2023 and 2025, while the team finished runners-up at the 2023 ODI World Cup and the World Test Championship.Having joined the national set-up in November 2021, Dilip's contract was not renewed after India's T20I tour of Zimbabwe, with Subhadeep Ghosh replacing him as fielding coach.
Article Summary: Former India fielding coach T Dilip has revealed what made Virat Kohli stand apart on the field, even at this stage of his career. Dilip said there was little difference between Kohli's approach during training and in matches. He also picked India's 2024 T20 World Cup triumph in Barbados as his most cherished moment with the team.

Article Title: World Athletics U-20 Championships: Bronze fine, but long jumper Shahnavaz Khan hoping for more
Article Text:
Shahnavaz Khan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOCHI: Shahnavaz Khan is a young man of few words, but his ambitions are anything but modest. He has never been one to celebrate average results, and even on Sunday, as India rejoiced over his bronze medal at the World Athletics U-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, he remained far from satisfied.His best effort of 7.84m, which earned him third place in the men’s long jump, did not meet the standards he had set for himself.“I am not satisfied with my jumps,” Shahnavaz told TOI over the phone from Eugene. “The first two jumps were fine, but after the third attempt I began to feel cramps,” added the 19-year old.The youngster revealed that his target at the Worlds had been to produce a new personal best.“Before every competition, I set a mark in my mind. Here, I wanted to improve my personal best, but I could not do it,” said Shahnavaz who trains at SAI Thiruvananthapuram under Bhupinder Singh.His disappointment was easy to understand. Shahnavaz had arrived at the championships as one of India’s strongest medal hopes, even a potential contender for gold, after delivering two outstanding performances earlier in the season.His biggest leap came at the National Inter-State Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar in June, where he jumped 8.30m to set a new under-20 national record. That effort came while competing alongside his training partner and India’s leading long jumper, Murali Sreeshankar Shahnavaz’s progress has been consistent. Last year, he claimed gold at the 38th National Games in February with a jump of 7.70m, and followed it with another gold at the Junior Federation Cup in June, where he recorded 7.90m.Tall, strong and muscular, he possesses the kind of explosive power at take-off that separates him from many leaner jumpers in his age group. Training with Sreeshankar has also played an important role in shaping his development.In Eugene, however, Shahnavaz could not find his best rhythm. He opened with 7.67m and 7.72m before registering his day’s best of 7.84m on the third attempt. His fifth jump appeared promising, but measured 7.83m, and he managed only 5.37m in the final round.Gold went to Italy’s Daniele Leonardo with 7.97m, leaving Shahnavaz to wonder what might have been had he approached his 8.30m personal best on the world stage.
Article Summary: Shahnavaz Khan came third in the men's long jump at the World Athletics U-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon. His best effort of 7.84m did not meet the standards he had set for himself. The 19-year-old said his target at the Worlds had been to produce a new personal best.

Article Title: Manas Dhamne, 18, gets Davis Cup call-up
Article Text:
Manas Dhamne (Image credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PUNE: Teenager Manas Dhamne’s rapid rise received a major endorsement on Monday when the 18-year-old was named in India’s squad for the Davis Cup Qualifier Round 2 tie vs South Korea on Sept 18-19.Dhamne, who hails from Satara, earned his call-up through consistent performances over the last two seasons. Ranked outside the top 1,000 in 2024, he climbed to No. 610 at the start of 2026 and is now ranked 362, making him the secondhighest-ranked Indian.The teenager trains under renowned coach Riccardo Piatti, who has previously worked with world No. 1 Jannik Sinner.Dhamne’s inclusion will strengthen a squad that also features Sumit Nagal (No. 235), Dhakshineswar Suresh (No. 393), and doubles pair of Yuki Bhambri and Sriram Balaji.Meanwhile, All India Tennis Association has retained Rohit Rajpal as captain despite growing concerns over his holding multiple positions in sports administration.India squad: Sumit Nagal, Manas Dhamne, D Suresh, Yuki Bhambri, Sriram Balaji. Reserve: Siddharth Rawat. Captain: Rohit Rajpal.
Article Summary: Manas Dhamne named in India’s squad for the Davis Cup Qualifier Round 2 tie vs South Korea on Sept 18-19. The 18-year-old earned his call-up through consistent performances over the last two seasons. He is now ranked 362, making him the secondhighest-ranked Indian.

Article Title: Hezly Rivera becomes first US woman after Simone Biles to win back-to-back gymnastics titles since 2012
Article Text:
Hezly Rivera

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Hezly Rivera has shown that she is no longer the young newcomer who surprised everyone at the Paris Olympics. The 18-year-old Olympic gold medallist won her second straight US women's gymnastics title after overcoming a fall on the uneven bars earlier in the competition. Rivera finished with a two-day total of 111.950 points, more than one point ahead of runner-up Claire Pease.Her victory made her the first American woman other than Simone Biles to win back-to-back national titles since former world and Olympic champion Jordyn Wieber achieved the feat in 2011 and 2012.From Olympic underdog to national championRivera described herself as an “underdog” two years ago when she was selected for the US Olympic team for Paris. She was the youngest and least-known member of a highly experienced team that won the women's team gold medal. It was the Americans' third team Olympic title in four Games.While several of her Olympic teammates, including Biles and Suni Lee, have taken extended breaks from competition, Rivera has continued to compete.Lee announced last month that she had started training again with the aim of returning to competition.Rivera won her first national title in New Orleans last year after edging Leanne Wong.Rivera's hopes of defending her title looked uncertain after she fell face-first onto the mat during the uneven bars competition on Thursday. She missed a release and could not stay on the apparatus. But Rivera responded strongly on the final day. She started Sunday on bars and produced a determined routine. She managed to recover from a small stall near the end before completing her dismount with a small step.Charleigh Bullock, who turned 16 last month, finished third. Reese Esponda, who trains at the Houston-area gym owned by Biles' family, took fourth place.Two-time Olympic gold medallist Jade Carey finished fifth.Carey is continuing to add difficulty to her routines as she targets a third appearance at the Olympic Games. The result also marked a homecoming for the Phoenix native.
Article Summary: Hezly Rivera won her second straight US women's gymnastics title. The 18-year- old overcame a fall on the uneven bars earlier in the competition. Rivera finished with a two-day total of 111.950 points, more than one point ahead of runner-up Claire Pease.

Article Title: Former Brazil international arrested after wife makes serious domestic violence allegation
Article Text:
Jadson has been arrested in Brazil following domestic violence allegations involving his wife, while the former Brazil international denies physical assault/Image: X

Jadson arrested after alleged domestic incident

Jadson denies physically assaulting his wife

Court grants provisional release

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Career with Brazil and Corinthians

Former Brazil international Jadson has been arrested in southern Brazil following allegations of domestic violence involving his wife. The 42-year-old, who enjoyed a successful career with clubs including Corinthians, Shakhtar Donetsk and Athletico Paranaense, has denied physically assaulting his partner, while Brazilian authorities continue to investigate the case after granting him provisional release under a series of court-imposed conditions.According to Globo Esporte , Jadson was arrested in the city of Cambé, in the southern Brazilian state of Paraná, following an alleged domestic violence incident that occurred during an argument with his wife.The outlet reported that the woman told police Jadson grabbed her by the neck with both hands and attempted to strangle her. Officers who responded to the incident reportedly observed visible marks on her neck that were consistent with her account.She also alleged that it was not the first time such an incident had occurred and requested protective measures as well as a medical injury assessment.Following his arrest, Jadson was initially taken to a police station before being transferred to Cambé State Prison.According to Globo Esporte, the former midfielder was formally investigated on suspicion of domestic violence, bodily harm and verbal abuse.During questioning by the Civil Police, Jadson acknowledged that an argument had taken place but denied using physical violence.According to Brazilian outlet Meu Timão, he described the incident as a marital dispute and insisted no physical assault had occurred.Both Jadson and the complainant were taken to the Central de Flagrantes police station without handcuffs before providing their statements to investigators.His legal team also issued a statement following the incident.According to Brazilian outlet Meu Timão , Jadson's defence said the investigation remains at an early stage and stressed that he is entitled to the presumption of innocence. The lawyers added that the court found no legal grounds to keep him in custody and said they would not discuss the case publicly while the investigation remains ongoing.According to Meu Timão, Judge Karin Feuerharmel Giuseppin, of the Londrina court, ordered Jadson's release on Sunday morning, granting him provisional freedom without requiring bail.The court imposed several precautionary measures while the investigation continues.Those conditions include reporting to the court every two months, informing authorities before leaving the city for more than 15 days, avoiding bars and similar establishments, and notifying the court of any change of address.The criminal investigation remains ongoing.Jadson retired from professional football in 2022, with his final club being Vitória.The attacking midfielder enjoyed successful spells with Shakhtar Donetsk, Corinthians and Athletico Paranaense, while also representing the Brazil national team.He was part of Brazil's squad that won the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup.At Corinthians, Jadson won the Brasileirão titles in 2015 and 2017, as well as the Campeonato Paulista in 2017, 2018 and 2019. He made 245 appearances for the club, scoring 50 goals and providing 64 assists.The case remains under investigation, and no final judicial determination has been made regarding the allegations against the former Brazil international.
Article Summary: Former Brazil international Jadson has been arrested in southern Brazil following allegations of domestic violence involving his wife. The 42-year-old, who enjoyed a successful career with clubs including Corinthians, Shakhtar Donetsk and Athletico Paranaense, has denied physically assaulting his partner. A court has granted him provisional release under a series of court-imposed conditions.

Article Title: Indian players counting on Women’s HIL experience at World Cup
Article Text:
(From left) Sunelita Toppo with Navneet Kaur and Kaitlin Nobbs during the Women's HIL early this year

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

When the Indian men’s hockey team ended a 41-year wait for an Olympic medal at Tokyo, the Hockey India League, which ran from 2013 to 2017, was cited as one of the factors behind the turnaround. Now, the women’s team too has something similar to draw experience from with the introduction of Women’s HIL last year.For the women, the biggest gain has been exposure — to foreign players, different styles of hockey and situations that are difficult to replicate during a national-team camp.“I think every player in our team has benefited from Women’s HIL. It has increased our confidence and helped us understand different match situations and movements,” said Lalremsiami, who will be playing in her third World Cup.For Neha, who played for Ranchi Royals in the last Women’s HIL, one of the biggest lessons came inside the opposition circle.“The players from other countries kept telling us that when we get into the D, we shouldn’t come out without trying something. We should keep looking for an opportunity and try to create something. I try to pass on those lessons to my teammates as well,” she said.That exchange of knowledge is perhaps even more significant for the younger members of the Indian squad.Sunelita Toppo, for instance, played alongside Navneet Kaur for SG Pipers, which won the 2026 Women’s HIL. It helped the two develop an understanding that they have now carried into the national team.“Sometimes, when I was running and trying to pass, the ball would go too fast or too slow, so the connection wasn’t always right. The strikers gave me feedback that if we could improve that connection, we could create better chances and score more goals,” said Sunelita.“I mostly link up with Navneet on the left, and they told me that if I could improve my body control and speed control, it would be a big benefit for the team. So, yes, I received that feedback and worked on it.”The benefit has gone beyond technical feedback. Playing together regularly has helped the pair develop an understanding that can sometimes make words unnecessary.“Sometimes you don’t even have to communicate verbally before making a pass because, through experience, you know where your teammate wants the ball and where she is likely to move,” added the youngster from Odisha.For another youngster, Sakshi Rana, the value of Women’s HIL lies in the experience of sharing the field and dressing room with senior players.“Our senior players keep sharing their experiences with us and motivating us. They tell us what they went through when they were our age and how they handled those situations,” said Sakshi.HIL, therefore, has become more than just another tournament on the calendar for the Indian women. It has created a bridge between domestic hockey and the demands of international competition. There is also a less visible benefit — financial security.For several players, particularly those from modest backgrounds, the league has provided an opportunity to earn significantly and support their families. That support can ease some of the pressures away from the field and allow them to focus more completely on hockey.
Article Summary: Women's Hockey India League has helped the Indian team gain exposure to foreign players, different styles of hockey and situations that are difficult to replicate during a national-team camp. The league has also provided an opportunity to earn significantly and support their families. The value of Women’s HIL lies in the experience of sharing the field and dressing room with senior players.

Article Title: From jumping a fence to World silver, 19-yr-old Basant Meghwal scripts history
Article Text:
Basant Meghwal (Image credit: X)

JAIPUR: For someone whose journey into athletics began under accidental circumstances — jumping over a fence while bunking school in his remote border Rajasthan village — Basant Kumar Meghwal’s silver effort at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon then is an extraordinary leap of faith.In what is proving a breakout season for the youngster, the 19-year-old Meghwal scripted history on Saturday by becoming the first Indian athlete to win a world high jump medal. He had also clinched gold at the Asian Under-20 Athletics Championships earlier this year.In Eugene, the podium finishers all maxed out at a height of 2.21 meters, meaning final placements were decided entirely by countback rules based on missed attempts. Algeria’s Younes Ayachi clinched gold by clearing the bar cleanly on his first attempt. Basant secured a momentous, personal-best silver for India by clearing the height on his second run, while Great Britain's Otis Poole took bronze on his third and final try.Meghwal’s run-up, though, begins differently. Not long ago, when he was in a field in his hamlet in Anupgarh tehsil of Sriganganagar district, lolling about the cattle instead of being in school, he spotted his physical training instructor, Iqbal Singh Maan, passing by.Fearing he would be caught skipping school, Basant leaped cleanly over a wire fence to hide.“His teacher saw that leap, immediately recognised his raw talent, and asked him to come to school instead. After that, he began to train him for the high jump,” father Gangaram Meghwal told TOI.“Before this happened, we didn't even know what high jump was or that such a sport existed.”The path to international glory required considerable sacrifices from the family. “We still carry a debt of around 3.5 lakh rupees because sports expenses are extremely high,” Meghwal Sr said, “I am a daily wage driver without any land of my own, earning around Rs 12,000-13,000 a month to raise my two children. I took loans from relatives and private lenders to finance Basant’s training, proper diet, and equipment.Just a single pair of high jump shoes costs Rs 15,000.”Despite the financial burden, Gangaram kept his son’s focus firmly on his craft. “I told him not to worry about the money, the loans will eventually be paid off. Focus on making a name for yourself. Today, seeing our child achieve a world medal brings us immense happiness,” said the proud father.Son Basant now represents the Indian Navy, a career move made through the sports quota entry. “When he started performing well, people guided us that it would secure his future,” his father added, “It changed everything for him, as it gave him a stable job and allowed him to pursue his athletic career without worrying about basic sustenance.”
Article Summary: Basant Kumar Meghwal won silver at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon. The 19-year-old became the first Indian athlete to win a world high jump medal. He had also clinched gold at the Asian Under-20 Athletics Championships earlier this year.

Article Title: ‘More practice days wouldn’t be as good’: Sitanshu Kotak’s bold claim after India’s warm-up win

India's batting coach Sitanshu Kotak. (ANI Photo)

‘Very good, very productive’

NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak believes the team gained more from its warm-up match against Sri Lanka than it could have from several additional days of conventional training, as the visitors completed a six-wicket win ahead of the Test series.Team India wrapped up its only practice fixture before the two-match series with a successful 207-run chase, giving players from both departments valuable match time ahead of the opening Test in Galle from August 15.Kotak was particularly impressed by the intensity on display, saying the competitive nature of the fixture made it more valuable than routine practice sessions.Speaking in a video shared by the BCCI on X, Kotak said: “I think it was very good, very productive because if we practice four more days, I don't think it will be as good as the practice match because the bowlers bowled with good intensity. He remained unbeaten on 142 off 164 balls as India declared their first innings at 357/6 in response to Sri Lanka XI's 363/8 declared.Kotak singled out Padikkal while also praising the contribution of India's fast bowlers on a pitch that offered little assistance.“I think Devdutt batted really well, the way Gurnoor also bowled, and our fast bowlers put a lot of effort on the wicket where there was nothing. All the pacers put in a lot of effort. I think it was all in all a very good practice match. I would say Gurnoor and Siraj hitting sixes, three to four-four sixes,” he added.Sri Lanka XI declared their second innings at 200/6 to set India 207. Yashasvi Jaiswal and Shubman Gill provided the platform before Ravindra Jadeja , Rishabh Pant and Siraj completed the chase.Gill, returning to action on the final day, scored a brisk 44 off 54 balls, while Siraj smashed an unbeaten 32 off just 15 balls, including four sixes.The result gives India valuable momentum and match practice before the Test series begins in Galle on August 15.

Article Title: Pratapgarh’s Shahnavaz scripts history, wins bronze at U-20 worlds
Article Text:
Shahnavaz Khan

LUCKNOW: Pratapgarh’s Shahnavaz Khan has become the first Indian man to win a long jump medal at the World Athletics U-20 Championships at Eugene, the US. Shaili Singh won silver in the women’s long jump in 2021. Shahnavaz clinched bronze in the men’s long jump with a best effort of 7.84m.Speaking to TOI from the US, an elated Shahnavaz said his athletics journey began near a canal in Sangrampur village in Pratapgarh, where he trained with local children and friends under senior athlete Mohd Hadees Khan.The 19-year-old said he later moved to Mumbai during the Covid period after taking admission to Pillai College of Engineering in Panvel. There, he trained under coach Imzamam-ul-Haq for two years before shifting in 2024 to the Sports Authority of India (SAI) centre in Trivandrum, where he is currently based.Reflecting on his achievement, Shahnavaz said he was aware of the significance of the medal. “I knew that before today, no Indian had ever won a medal in the men’s long jump category at the U-20 World Championship. This medal is not just mine, it belongs to the country.I am going to the Asian Games in September, and I will finish on the podium there,” he said.Shahnavaz added that he was unable to produce his personal best because of fitness concerns. “I had an injury on my right side and was also dealing with cramps, so I could not deliver my personal best. Just last month in July, I won gold at the Junior Asian Athletics Championships with the same mark of 7.84, and today I achieved 7.84 again.My personal best is 8.30, which I recorded at the Inter-State Athletics Championship,” he said.The athlete credited his uncle, Sharukh, a steeplechase runner, as a major source of inspiration. “My motivation to win medals comes from my uncle, Sharukh, who is a steeplechase athlete. He set a record last year, and whenever he returned with a medal, it inspired me and made me feel that I would bring one home too,” Khan said.UP Athletics Association secretary Narendra praised Shahnavaz Khan. He said, “My best wishes are with the athletes. They put up good results on the wall.”
Article Summary: Pratapgarh’s Shahnavaz Khan has become the first Indian man to win a long jump medal at the World Athletics U-20 Championships at Eugene, the US. The 19-year- old clinched bronze in the men's long jump with a best effort of 7.84m. He trained under coach Imzamam-ul-Haq for two years.

Article Title: World Athletics U20 Championships: India end campaign with three-medal haul
Article Text:
L-R: Basant Kumar Meghwal, Ashish Yadav and Shahnavaz Khan (AFI Photos)

India finish with two silver, one bronze

India continue to build U20 medal record

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's campaign at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Oregon, USA, ended with three medals after high jumper Pooja Singh finished seventh in the women's final, falling well short of the national senior record that had raised expectations around her title bid.The 19-year-old Pooja could clear only 1.84m in the final and failed in all three attempts at 1.87m. Her performance was below the 1.93m national senior record she set while winning gold at the Asian U20 Athletics Championships in May.Pooja, who is also the reigning Senior Asian Athletics Championships gold medallist, had entered the competition as one of India's leading medal hopes.Australia's Izobelle Louison-Roe won the gold with a clearance of 1.92m. Hungary's Lilianna Batori and Spain's Aitana Alonso both cleared 1.90m, with Batori taking silver and Alonso bronze.India's women's 4x400m relay team also ended its campaign with a ninth-place finish in the final. Bhoomika Nehate, Tahura Khatun, Tanu Chaudhary and Thiya Arumugam clocked 3:45.28 to finish last.The United States won gold in 3:29.15, followed by Australia (3:31.39) and Great Britain (3:32.08).India's three-medal haul comprised two silver and one bronze, matching the country's medal tally from the 2021 and 2022 editions of the championships.Ashish Yadav opened India's medal count with silver in the men's javelin throw, before Basant Kumar Meghwal added another silver in the men's high jump. Shahnavaz Khan then secured bronze in the men's long jump.While the campaign ended without a gold medal, the three-medal haul underlined India's improved consistency at the global junior level.Between 2002 and 2018, India won only four medals at the World Athletics U20 Championships. Those included historic gold medals from Neeraj Chopra in the men's javelin throw in 2016 and Hima Das in the women's 400m in 2018.Discus thrower Seema Antil won India's first medal at the championships, taking silver in 2002, while Navjeet Kaur Dhillon added bronze in the same event in 2014.India subsequently won three medals in 2021, including silver medals for Amit in the men's 10,000m race walk and Shaili Singh in the women's long jump, besides a bronze in the mixed 4x400m relay.The 2022 edition brought three more medals, with Selva Prabhu Thirumaran and the mixed 4x400m relay team winning silver and Rupal Chaudhary taking bronze.India managed only one medal in the 2024 edition, with Aarti winning bronze in the women's 10,000m race walk.The three-medal haul in the latest edition therefore represents a return to the stronger medal returns of 2021 and 2022.
Article Summary: India finish with two silver, one bronze at World Athletics U20 Championships. High jumper Pooja Singh fails to clear 1.84m in the women's final. India's women's 4x400m relay team also finishes ninth in the final.

Article Title: Young spinners prepare to take over from Nathan Lyon

CHENNAI: With Australia’s development squad sweating it out in Chennai, their next generation of spin bowlers are getting a taste of what it takes to succeed in conditions vastly different from home. For left-arm spinner Joel Davies, leg-spinner Lloyd Pope and off-spinner Jack Sinfield, the challenge is not just about making an impression in India but also pushing their claims for a place in the national setup. So, I think he’ll keep hanging around while he’s still fit. But I think there are some very good options around state cricket at the moment,” he said.Australia selector Tony Dodemaide had earlier described Davies to TOI as “a very exciting prospect”.

Article Title: 'Difficult assignment': PCB advised to 'keep away' Babar Azam from English media on England tour
Article Text:
Babar Azam

Former Pakistan captain Rashid Latif has suggested that the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) should keep Babar Azam away from the English media during the team’s upcoming three-Test tour of England.Latif believes Babar could come under scrutiny from the English media and has suggested that former Pakistan captain Shan Masood should handle more of the team’s media interactions during the series.“An England tour is a difficult assignment, and the English media often tries to unnecessarily involve visiting teams in news stories,” Rashid said while speaking to Geo News.“Babar Azam is an experienced player, so it would be better for the PCB management to keep him away from the English media and send former captain Shan Masood to speak to them more often,” he added.“Shan has played in England and has better experience of dealing with the English media,” Rashid said.Latif’s comments came after Babar made an important contribution during Pakistan’s recent two-Test series against the West Indies.Babar remained unbeaten on 58 in Pakistan’s 90-run defeat in the first Test at the Brian Lara Stadium in Tarouba. Pakistan were bowled out for 120 while chasing 211, with Babar left unbeaten as the rest of the batting order collapsed.Babar then scored 88 off 147 balls in Pakistan’s first innings of the second Test at Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain. His innings helped Pakistan reach 387 after the West Indies had scored 344.He followed it with an unbeaten 24 off 30 balls in the second innings as Pakistan chased down 75 to win by eight wickets and level the series 1-1.The victory ended Pakistan’s eight-match losing streak in away Tests and gave Babar his first overseas Test win since returning as captain.Pakistan will now prepare for their England tour, with the first Test scheduled to begin at Headingley in Leeds on August 19. The second Test will be played at Lord’s from August 27, while the series will conclude at Edgbaston from September 9.
Article Summary: Babar Azam could come under scrutiny from the English media, says Rashid Latif. Former captain Shan Masood should handle more of the team's media interactions during the series. Babar made an important contribution during Pakistan’s recent two-Test series against the West Indies.

Article Title: Sandeep Lamichhane returns as Nepal ODI captain, replaces Rohit Paudel

Nepal eye another Premier Cup triumph

Nepal have made a major leadership change ahead of the ACC Men’s Premier Cup, with leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane returning as the country’s ODI captain. The Cricket Association of Nepal announced the 26-year-old as Rohit Paudel ’s replacement while naming the squad for the tournament in Malaysia from August 30 to September 12.Lamichhane previously led Nepal in 14 ODIs before Paudel took over in 2022. He brings plenty of experience to the role, having taken 154 wickets in 77 ODIs. He is also Nepal’s fastest bowler to 150 ODI wickets and the first player from the country to take more than 100 T20I wickets.Paudel leaves the captaincy after an impressive spell in charge. Under his leadership, Nepal produced a remarkable run in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2, winning 11 of their final 12 matches and earning direct qualification for the 2023 ODI World Cup Qualifier in Zimbabwe. He was also an important middle-order batter for the team.Lamichhane’s return to the leadership role signals a fresh start for Nepal as they aim to strengthen their 50-over cricket. The squad also features several changes, with Kushal Bhurtel, Bhim Sharki, Nandan Yadav and Binod Bhandari left out. Sompal Kami and Aarif Sheikh return, while Dev Khanal, Sher Malla, Sundeep Jora and Basir Ahamad have been added.The 2026 tournament will be the third edition of the ACC Men’s Premier Cup and will be played in the 50-over format. Nepal won the inaugural edition in 2023 as hosts.Nepal squad: Sandeep Lamichhane (c), Aasif Sheikh, Arjun Kumal, Rohit Paudel, Dev Khanal, Dipendra Singh Airee, Sundeep Jora, Basir Ahamad, Ishan Pandey, Gulsan Jha, Sher Malla, Lalit Rajbanshi, Karan KC, Hemant Dhami.

Article Title: PCB keeps central contracts list under wraps amid new format-based system
Article Text:
Babar Azam

The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) is yet to take a final decision on whether it will publicly announce the list of players who will receive central contracts under its new payment and categorisation system.The PCB usually announces its list of centrally contracted players by the first week of August. The contracts normally run from June to July every fiscal year.“The thinking is that it is not necessary to announce the players who are to be given these new contracts, as it is an internal matter of the board,” a source was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.Pakistan ODI captain Shaheen Shah Afridi was asked about the issue during a media interaction in Multan on Monday but said he was not aware of the development.The PCB had earlier confirmed that it would introduce format-based central contracts for the 2026-27 period. Under the new system, male players will be eligible for contracts if they have played at least four Tests, six ODIs or as many T20Is in the previous 12 months.The new format-based system has also made it difficult for the board to decide which categories individual players should be placed in, PTI reported, quoting source.The uncertainty over the contracts comes at a time when the PCB is also facing questions over its financial disclosures.Last week, the PCB secured a stay order from the Islamabad High Court until September 22 after a government agency asked the board to provide financial and other details of its accounts.The current PCB administration, headed by Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, has not regularly made its financial information public. Since 2023, the board has not published audited statements on its website, although doing so had previously been a regular practice.The PCB has shared financial details with the media only when it has considered the information useful to its interests.
Article Summary: The Pakistan Cricket Board is yet to take a final decision on whether it will publicly announce the list of players who will receive central contracts. The PCB usually announces its list of centrally contracted players by the first week of August. The contracts normally run from June to July every fiscal year.

Article Title: ‘Huge credit to him’: VVS Laxman recalls Jay Shah’s role in driving BCCI CoE project
Article Text:
VVS Laxman and Jay Shah

The Board of Control for Cricket in India’s (BCCI) Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru is nearing its second anniversary, with BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia recalling the work that went into setting up the facility.Saikia credited former BCCI secretary Jay Shah, who is now the International Cricket Council (ICC) chairman, with pushing the project and bringing officials together to ensure it was completed."He took everybody on board in BCCI's Apex Council and made a firm decision that this establishment (CoE) has to be done on a war footing, and we need to move on from the old, temporary arrangement of National Cricket Academy," Saikia told select media at the BCCI CoE.Laxman, Head of Cricket at CoE, recalled moving from Hyderabad to Bengaluru in 2021 after Shah and then BCCI president Sourav Ganguly approached him."In 2021, when Jay and then BCCI president Sourav (Ganguly) reached out to me, saying that Rahul (Dravid) is moving to the Indian team as the head coach, and we want that continuity.""It was a tough decision for me. But as a cricketer, I always thought that it's the responsibility of former cricketers who benefited through this great game to contribute back to the game.And with that intention, obviously, I moved to Bangalore in December 2021," he said.Laxman also recalled Shah's involvement in the project and his regular participation in meetings with the architects and L&T team."In the span of close to two years, the entire infrastructure was up and running. And huge credit to Jay, because he was the secretary of the BCCI and I myself seen firsthand how much interest he used to take in various meetings we used to have with the architects, with the L&T team, to make sure that each and every aspect of the COE, or then NCA, is taken care of."And it's great to see that, you know, the vision was translated into reality. And I think all leaders have vision. But the vision will only bear the fruit when it's translated into reality. And that reality is what we've seen in 2024, November," he said.
Article Summary: BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru nearing its second anniversary. Devajit Saikia credits former BCCI secretary Jay Shah with pushing the project. VVS Laxman recalls moving from Hyderabad to Bengaluru in 2021 after Shah and then BCCI president Sourav Ganguly approached him.

Article Title: Trial by spin with a hint of reverse: Inside India's final net session in Colombo
Article Text:
Sarfaraz Khan joined the India Test squad as a replacement for Sai Sudharsan in Sri Lanka. (Image: TimesofIndia.com)

TimesofIndia.com in Colombo:

India Test captain Shubman Gill during the nets in Colombo. (Image: TimesofIndia.com)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ravindra Jadeja sports a new sticker on his bat in Colombo. (Image: TimesofIndia.com)

Sarfaraz Khan beamed when he got off the team bus on Monday. There were greetings exchanged with members of the support staff on the bus before the 28-year-old, who joined the squad as a replacement for Sai Sudharsan , got down to business. After a quick huddle and pep talk, the team executed a meticulous plan and everyone seemed aware of the objectives for the session under the unforgiving sun.The centre wicket, baking under the sun, was ready for a trial by spin and head coach Gautam Gambhir got into a good vantage point to observe proceedings. The batters played as per the expected batting order in Galle and rotation occurred to break monotony and put concentration levels to test. The spin quartet of Ravindra Jadeja , Kuldeep Yadav, Manav Suthar and Saransh Jain did the bulk of the bowling as only Auqib Nabi was there to do to the fast bowling lifting.On a pitch resembling what would have been a Day 4 pitch of the warm-up game which concluded on Sunday , the Indian team management tried to create an experience similar to what is expected in the upcoming series. The strip was dry, had enough cracks and batting from just one end meant it only got more difficult as the session progressed - just like in a Test match.There was variety in the type of balls used, mixing old, new and semi-new ones. Nabi, in particular, bowled with a lot of heart, as the rest of the fast bowlers - Mohammed Siraj, Gurnoor Brar and Prasidh Krishna - were given a much-needed rest after the multi-day fixture. Captain Shubman Gill was aware that one fast bowler wouldn't be enough to give him the desired volume of practice so he went to the practice nets with the throwdown specialists and batting coach Sitanshu Kotak.The plan was simple. One new ball and two oldish balls, be prepared to face some reverse swing. Plenty of deliveries were fired at the right-hander who looked largely in control except for a few balls which rose awkwardly or kept a tad low. Between the good leaves and exquisite cover drives, the shouts of "shot, Gill", "well left, Gill" kept the mood going before the Indian captain left the area to occupy the centre wicket with India's No.3 Devdutt Padikkal.Every Indian batter took their time adjusting to the roughed up surface and was allowed to flex their muscle towards the end of their hit. There were plenty of long strides, solid defences, tentative prods and a mix of sweeps and reverse-sweeps during the session which lasted well over three hours. Between the plans, executions and drills, there was enough time for banter too.Ravindra Jadeja showed his new bat sticker, inspired by his pet horse, and Sarfaraz flexed his biceps to show his improved fitness levels. The Bengaluru boys Padikkal and KL Rahul, enjoyed each other's company and the massage table remained busy as almost every player got a nice stretch after their respective session.For the last six days, India have been coming daily to the NCC Ground in Colombo. A mix of the multi-day fixture and net sessions - starting at different times - ensured the team is well prepared before reaching Galle for the series opener on August 15. The Indian team is set to reach Galle on August 11 and will have three more sessions before the coin goes up for a toss at the historic Galle International Stadium.
Article Summary: The spin quartet of Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav, Manav Suthar and Saransh Jain did the bulk of the bowling as only Auqib Nabi was there to do to the fast bowling lifting. Captain Shubman Gill was aware that one fast bowler wouldn't be enough to give him the desired volume of practice so he went to the practice nets with the throwdown specialists.

Article Title: 'Creates uncertainty, disrupts planning': Associate nations take aim at ICC over ODI World Cup format changes
Article Text:
ICC chairperson Jay Shah (left), and Men's ODI World Cup trophy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cricket Scotland and the Royal Dutch Cricket Association (KNCB) on Monday criticised the International Cricket Council’s recent changes to the qualification pathway and format for the Men’s 50-over World Cup.The two European Associate Member boards said they were disappointed that the ICC had made what they described as “significant structural changes” less than 18 months before the tournament."Cricket Scotland and the Royal Dutch Cricket Association (KNCB) are deeply disappointed by the International Cricket Council's recent decision to implement significant structural changes to the ICC Men's 50-over World Cup qualification pathway and tournament format with less than 18 months until the competition begins," the two boards said in a joint statement.The ICC announced the changes in June as part of a revamp of the structures for its two men's World Cup tournaments. The changes include the introduction of 'Super Series' and 'Super 7' rounds at next year's 50-over World Cup.The tournament will still have 14 teams, as previously planned. However, the three lowest-ranked teams will now first play in a 'Super Series' round. Only the team that finishes top of that round will advance to the main 12-team group stage.From the main group phase, the top three teams from each group, along with the next best-placed team across the two groups, will advance to the new 'Super 7' round.Scotland and the Netherlands said the changes could affect the growth of Associate Member cricket."These changes represent a setback to Associate Member cricket and risk undermining the progress made in recent years to grow the global game."They also questioned the timing and consultation process behind the changes."Decisions of this significance, particularly those directly affecting Associate Members, should be made clearly following meaningful consultation and with sufficient notice for affected Members to understand and respond to the implications. The timing of these changes, with less than eighteen months until the tournament, has given affected Members limited opportunity to contribute to the process or adapt. We believe greater engagement with Associate Members would have supported a more effective and collaborative approach and help maintain confidence in the qualification pathway," the joint statement added.The two boards said changing qualification rules during a cycle creates uncertainty for players and teams."Members and their players invest years in preparing for World Cups, and confidence in those pathways depends on them not changing part-way through a qualification cycle without consultation. Changing those structures at short notice creates significant uncertainty, disrupts planning, and places additional operational and financial pressure on organisations that are already operating with limited resources," the statement further said.They also highlighted the importance of World Cup participation for Associate Members."The opportunity to compete at a World Cup provides Associate Members with a unique competitive opportunity to drive investment, inspire players, attract commercial partners and government support, and create moments that capture the imagination of supporters. Some of the most memorable moments in ICC tournaments have come when Associate Members have challenged, and in some cases defeated, Full Members on the world stage. Those performances have always reinforced the principle that success is earned on the field. Our players work incredibly hard with limited resources to earn these opportunities and deserve respect and for their efforts to be rewarded."The boards said providing Associate Members with opportunities to qualify for major tournaments was important if cricket wanted to expand globally."Leaders in cricket have consistently spoken about their ambition for the sport to become truly global. Providing meaningful opportunities for emerging nations to qualify for and compete at major events is fundamental to achieving that ambition. Decisions that reduce or limit those opportunities slow the progress being made to expand the game's reach and appeal and runs counter to those ambitions," it added.
Article Summary: The ICC announced the changes in June as part of a revamp of the structures for its two men's World Cup tournaments. Article Title: 6 balls, 6 sixes: Batter unleashes stunning power-hitting blitz in county match
Article Text:
Toby Albert (Image credit: Hampshire Cricket)

Albert's six-sixes burst

Mayes, Orr provide the platform

Albert continues impressive form

NEW DELHI: Six balls, six sixes, pure mayhem. Six maximums from six deliveries is one of the rarest sights in cricket. Hampshire batter Toby Albert produced exactly that stunning sequence during the One-Day Cup clash against Sussex in Hove on Sunday, turning the game on its head with a breathtaking display of power-hitting.Albert's six sixes came across two overs and helped Hampshire post a massive 383-9. He smashed 86 off just 37 balls as Hampshire went on to beat Sussex by 51 runs.It was Hampshire's second-highest List A total, behind their 396-5 against Kent in Beckenham in 2022. The 383 also equalled the highest team total in the 2026 One-Day Cup so far, with Lancashire having scored 389-4 against Leicestershire.Hampshire eventually secured their fourth win of the season after beating Sussex by 51 runs.Albert came to the crease with around 15 overs left and quickly changed the pace of the innings.The remarkable sequence began with the last two balls of the 43rd over, bowled by Nantes Oosthuizen. The two sixes took Albert to his fifty from only 26 balls. He then took on Ollie Kirtley and smashed four more sixes in a row to complete six maximums from six consecutive deliveries.Albert ended his innings with 86 off just 37 balls. His 26-ball fifty was also the fastest 50-plus score in this year's One-Day Cup.Hampshire were already in a strong position before Albert launched his attack.Ben Mayes marked his first appearance of the season with a 109 off 115 balls, registering his maiden List A century. His opening partner Ali Orr also scored a hundred, making 105 off 100 balls. The pair put on 225 runs in 35 overs before Albert came in at No. 3 and took the scoring rate even higher.Sussex unable to chase 384Sussex suffered an early setback in their chase after Tom Haines and Oli Carter were dismissed cheaply. Charlie Tear kept the hosts in the contest with a 111 off 94 balls. Jack Leaning and Danial Ibrahim also contributed half-centuries.But Sussex were eventually bowled out for 332, giving Hampshire a 51-run victory. It was Sussex's sixth defeat in seven matches this season.Albert has scored 221 runs from three matches in the tournament, including two fifties. His best score so far is 89, which came in Hampshire's defeat against Durham in Southampton.Across his List A career, the right-hander has scored 962 runs in 26 innings at an average of 43.72, with seven half-centuries.Hampshire will face Derbyshire in Southampton on August 11. A victory will confirm their place in the quarter-finals.
Article Summary: Hampshire batter Toby Albert hit six sixes in just two overs. He smashed 86 off just 37 balls as Hampshire beat Sussex by 51 runs. It was Hampshire's second- highest List A total, behind 396-5 against Kent in 2022.

Article Title: Australia U-19’s Neel Patel ready to embrace India challenge: 'The wickets will be quite different' | Exclusive
Article Text:
Australian U-19 all-rounder Neel Patel with his family. (Photo Courtesy: Cricket NSW)

New Delhi:

Neel Patel standing at the back in left corner with other Australia U-19 cricketers. (Photo Courtesy: Cricket Australia)

Some of the Australian players, like Ricky Ponting and Steve Smith, when I was growing up were my idols. Neel Patel

Neel Patel also bowls off-spin. (Photo courtesy: Cricket Australia)

Neel is among the 16 selected to travel for three one-day matches and two four-day games in Rajkot and Ahmedabad, respectively, starting September 13. (Photo Courtesy: Cricket Australia)

With the four-day game, I want to understand the pace of the game, how to play it and just enjoy the four-day experience. Neel Patel

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Neel Patel's first cricketing memory isn't a cricket ground. It is the balcony of his family's apartment in Australia, where his grandfather would bowl underarm to him and Patel, armed with a plastic foam bat, would try to hit the ball as hard as he could.It was simple, almost instinctive. There was no talk of technique, roles or long-term plans. There was just a child, a bat and a ball.That uncomplicated relationship with cricket has remained central to Patel's development, even as the game around him has become increasingly serious. Now part of Australia's Under-19 setup, the 17-year-old is looking ahead to the long tour of India, one that offers him a chance to test his game in conditions markedly different from those he has grown up playing in."It’s definitely going to be a really nice experience playing in India, especially in the hot conditions compared to Australia," Patel tells TimesofIndia.com from Sydney. "The wickets will be quite different, so it's about learning to adapt to the conditions and the bowlers as well."Neel is among the 16 selected to travel for three one-day matches and two four-day games in Rajkot and Ahmedabad, respectively, starting September 13.For a young cricketer, the attraction of India is obvious. For Patel, it carries another layer. His father Punit Patel moved to Australia in 2001, and Neel was born there in 2009. Cricket, therefore, has always occupied a space between two cultures, though he does not describe his upbringing as particularly unusual."I think it was quite normal, actually," he says. "There are quite a lot of Indians in Sydney, and obviously lots of Australians as well. So I think it was quite a normal childhood."Neel's earliest memory of watching cricket came during the 2015 World Cup in Australia, when his family and friends went to the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for one of the matches. By then, the child playing with a foam bat on a balcony had begun absorbing the sights and sounds of international cricket.There were Australian influences too. Ricky Ponting and Steve Smith were among the players he admired while growing up. Patel also found inspiration in Indian cricketers, watching them and taking from their games the same quality he wanted to develop in his own: fearlessness."Some of the Australian players, like Ricky Ponting when I was growing up, and Steve Smith," he says on who influenced his cricket. "There were obviously some Indian cricketers as well. I enjoyed watching them play. They inspired me to enjoy the game and play fearlessly."Patel's own cricketing identity has evolved considerably. As a youngster, he was a genuine all-rounder. He opened the batting and bowled frontline spin in underage and representative cricket. He also experimented with pace in club cricket, sometimes bowling one over of spin and the next of pace simply because he enjoyed doing everything.Eventually, however, his batting began to demand more attention. Last year, Neel became one of the youngest players to score more than 1000 runs in Sydney Premier Cricket in a calendar year."As I progressed into grade cricket, they realised my batting potential," he says. "The next season, I opened the batting and from there I started prioritising batting a little bit more because I enjoyed it as well and was getting a lot of success from it."The bowling has stayed. Off-spin became his preferred discipline after he found himself taking wickets with it and enjoying the craft. His father helped him work on it, and Patel saw an opportunity to make the two disciplines complement each other."I began getting quite good at it, so we stuck with it," he says. "It also complemented my batting, so it wasn't too much of a stretch."But the India tour is likely to test the batting side of his game more closely. Patel knows that conditions in India can expose technical limitations that might remain hidden elsewhere.He has already played in Delhi, Bengaluru and Jaipur, and has noticed the difference from Australia. Less grass, flatter wickets, low bounce and the influence of spin create a different examination for a batter."In India, it's quite hot and the wickets have less grass and aren't as bouncy. They favour batters and spinners much more," he says. "I think India is definitely a good place to learn how to play spin, particularly, and how to bat in tough conditions when it's really hot and you have to bat for long periods."That is where his current development work comes in.Patel identified that his front-foot game was already a strength and decided to spend more time developing his back-foot play. The objective was not simply to add shots, but to become harder to contain."I thought, 'Why not focus on my back-foot game a little bit more in the off-season to become a complete batter?'" he says.The thinking is particularly relevant in India, where bowlers may not offer the same opportunities to drive through the front of the wicket. Patel wants to be able to access more areas of the ground when the ball is delivered shorter."Working on my back-foot game allows me to access all parts of the ground much better," he says. "I can play all types of shots, both front-foot and back-foot."There is a similar sense of purpose in how he approaches the wider development of his game. Patel says he is not particularly superstitious. Instead, he keeps short and long-term goals to give his training a clear direction."It helps me have a purpose when I'm training and playing, and it helps me stay accountable for what I'm doing," he says.That mindset could prove valuable on a tour that demands adaptation. Alongside the four-day game, Patel will have the opportunity to experience a different rhythm of cricket, different bowling styles and the challenge of spending an extended period away from home.He is not arriving in India with the expectation of having everything figured out. He is arriving to learn."With the four-day game, I want to understand the pace of the game, how to play it and just enjoy the four-day experience," he says.For the boy who once tried to smash underarm deliveries from his grandfather on an apartment balcony, the journey has moved a long way. But the essence remains familiar: bat in hand, ball coming towards him, and the instinct to find a way to hit it.Only now, the challenge is much bigger. And for Patel, India represents another opportunity to discover how far his game can travel.
Article Summary: Australian U-19 all-rounder Neel Patel is part of Australia's tour of India. The 17-year-old is among the 16 selected to travel for three one-day matches and two four-day games in Rajkot and Ahmedabad, starting September 13. His father Punit Patel moved to Australia in 2001, and Neel was born there in 2009.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing
